other_official_servers: The vendor describes a local MCP server connection using an API key for custom integrations, but does not document a separate endpoint or its tool list: https://www.privacy.com/blog/privacy-mcp-connect-ai-assistant-privacy-account

B_access_pricing.mcp_access_cost_details: The MCP page says a paid Privacy Plan is required for API access. The pricing page lists Plus at $5/month ($60/year billed annually) as the first plan with API Access; Pro is $10/month ($120/year), and Premium is $25/month ($300/year). The Personal plan is $0 and does not list API Access.
B_access_pricing.linked_software_cost: Personal: $0; Plus: $5/month or $60/year; Pro: $10/month or $120/year; Premium: $25/month or $300/year.
B_access_pricing.pricing_model_details: Subscription tiers include different monthly card creation limits: 12 Personal, 24 Plus, 36 Pro, 60 Premium. MCP access is linked to the paid plan’s API Access. The pages reviewed do not specify a separate MCP fee or per-call charge.
B_access_pricing.other_access_restrictions: The endpoint requires authentication. OAuth is documented; for clients without MCP OAuth support, the vendor documents using a PRIVACY_API_KEY. No MCP-specific rate limit, client allowlist, region restriction, or admin switch was found.
B_access_pricing.restrictions_controlled_by: Vendor controls plan entitlement and OAuth/API access; the user selects a plan and authorizes account access.

It publishes brief descriptions and parameter summaries, but no input schemas, annotations, or tool output schemas.

C_capabilities.authorization_mechanism: OAuth is the documented hosted flow. The endpoint’s protected-resource metadata identifies authorization server https://api.app.privacy.com. Its authorization-server metadata lists response_types_supported ["code"], grant_types_supported ["authorization_code","refresh_token"], code_challenge_methods_supported ["S256"], scopes_supported ["mcp:tools"], token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported ["none"], and registration_endpoint https://api.app.privacy.com/oauth/register. It also lists revocation_endpoint https://api.app.privacy.com/oauth/revoke. Token lifetime is not provided. The endpoint returned HTTP 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="Missing Authorization header", resource_metadata="https://mcp.privacy.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource".

D_server_side_logic.additional_logic: 1. The official tool page marks no read-only/destructive/idempotent/open-world annotations. By operation, list_cards, get_card, get_pan, and list_transactions are reads; create_card, pause_card, unpause_card, close_card, update_card_memo, and update_card_spend_limit write or change state. 2. No server-enforced per-action confirmation, confirm parameter, preview flow, elicitation, or approval workflow is documented. The docs warn that users are responsible for financial activity. 3. OAuth supports the advertised mcp:tools scope; paid-plan API access is required. Inheritance of product roles, organization admin controls, client allowlists, redirect approval and token lifetime are not documented. Revocation endpoint is advertised. 4. No read-only mode, tool filter, query-free mode, sandbox/production split, or regional variant was found in reviewed docs. 5. get_pan returns full PAN, CVV and expiration per the official description; no MCP masking or field-level boundary is documented. 6. Pagination is documented: list_cards page_size 1–100 (default 20); list_transactions page_size 1–1000 (default 20). No MCP rate limit, bulk cap, truncation, or per-call price found. 7. Parameter summaries and enum choices are published; server-side unknown-argument rejection, coercion, corrections, or operator overrides are not documented. 8. MCP-specific audit events, logging, telemetry and opt-out are not documented. 9. The official 10-tool list and Claude listing contain no feedback/rating/report/survey tool. No tool-result upsell or marketing elicitation is documented. 10. The MCP page does not publish server-delivered skills or agent instructions beyond setup and the financial-responsibility warning. 11. No memory or cross-call state behavior documented. 12. No hierarchy, proxying, or nested agent architecture documented for the hosted endpoint. 13. No raw API, arbitrary SQL, script execution, or general escape-hatch tool appears in the official tool list.

E_aggregated.human_can_agent_cannot: The developer API documentation lists operations absent from the MCP tools: share a card by email, list funding sources, and check API status. The broader product supports card features such as Category-Locked and Everywhere Cards, while the MCP create_card type options shown are SINGLE_USE, MERCHANT_LOCKED, and UNLOCKED. The CLI separately documents create-card types SINGLE_USE and MERCHANT_LOCKED. F_documentation.implementation_hints_not_enforced: The documentation tells users to authorize OAuth or provide an API key in unsupported clients; these are connection instructions. The financial-responsibility warning is a statement to the user, not a documented server-side confirmation gate. No behavioral guidance to the AI beyond the warning was found.
F_documentation.governance_promises: The blog states: “Privacy has not integrated AI into our platform in any way that accesses, analyzes, or uses your card data or account activity” and “We are not feeding them into AI models.” It describes MCP as a tool users choose to connect to their own assistant. The privacy policy says Privacy collects and uses the minimum data necessary for compliance and service delivery, does not sell user information for advertising or marketing, and describes security controls including encryption and annual PCI/SOC 2 certifications. These are vendor statements; MCP-specific retention or training terms were not found.
F_documentation.promises_to_user: The official MCP description says it lets connected AI assistants take actions or retrieve information on the user’s behalf. The blog frames the connection as optional and user-controlled. The vendor warns that users remain responsible for financial activity initiated through MCP.
F_documentation.comparison_with_server_logic: The financial responsibility warning is text-only in the reviewed materials; no per-action confirmation mechanism is documented. OAuth is backed by public authorization metadata, and plan gating is stated in official docs/pricing. The blog’s AI-use statements concern Privacy’s platform and data use; they do not specify how a separately connected AI provider processes MCP results.

contradictions: The MCP docs say paid Privacy Plan/API access is required, and the pricing page places API Access in Plus and above. The blog’s phrase “Customers on our Plus ($5/month) plan and above have API access” is consistent with this, though its nearby wording “API access is required” is less specific about the paid tier.

The MCP create_card reference lists UNLOCKED as a supported card type, while the CLI create command documents only SINGLE_USE and MERCHANT_LOCKED. These are different documented interfaces; the docs do not explain the discrepancy.

The MCP tool list lacks share-card, funding-source, and API-status operations that appear in the developer API reference. This is a difference in exposed MCP surface, not evidence that those operations are unavailable through other interfaces.
observations_for_research: The endpoint is globally addressed and requires OAuth; its metadata advertises one scope, mcp:tools, covering tool access.
The official tool list includes both card mutation operations and a get_pan tool that returns full payment-card credentials.
The documentation makes financial accountability explicit but does not document a required confirmation parameter or server-side approval gate for writes.
